source_read: PMC HTML (PMC4988731; Schizophrenia Bulletin 2016;42(5):1262-1269), the published version (courtesy of Oxford University Press; no author-manuscript banner), read in my own browser tab on 2026-10-31 (title checked), start to end: abstract, Introduction, Methods (search strategy; selection criteria and data extraction; statistical analysis with Table 1), Results, Discussion, funding, conflict statement, reference list. Figures 1-3 are images and were viewed on screen at the figure pages' full resolution (Figure 1 flow diagram; Figure 2 fitted curves per study; Figure 3 forest plots with each study's estimate and the subgroup totals). The supplementary files (a .doc and an index page) were not opened, as the brief requires.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of Marconi's result; three precision points. (1) 'Against never use': the Methods say never users were always the reference, but Table 1's reference rows read 'No cannabis within last year' (Wiles), 'None' or 'No use' for frequency of use at baseline (Henquet, Degenhardt) and 'No cannabis use at age 18' (Arseneault); 'against no use (never, or none in the period each study measured)' would match the table. (2) 3.90 is the fitted odds ratio at the very top of the ranking (x = 1, the single heaviest-ranked person in each study), not the odds for a top category as a group; the paper gives 3.40 (2.55-4.54) for the median person in the top 20% and 1.97 (1.68-2.31) for the median person who used at all, and says its estimate is for the most severe user, not the average user in the top category. (3) Understatement: 'no source read gives absolute risks by level of use' is not quite true of this source. Table 1 prints cases and totals at every level, so crude absolute risks can be read off for the six cohorts (editors' calculation, unadjusted; follow-up lengths are not given here): Swedish conscripts, admission for schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 (0.59%) with no use vs 28 of 731 (3.8%) with more than 50 occasions; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder at 26, 12 of 494 (2.4%) vs 3 of 29 (10.3%).
claims.note: Every number from this source checked and matching: 10 studies, 66,816 people (Table 1 rows sum to 66,816, editors' calculation); pooled b 1.36 (1.04-1.68), OR 3.90 (2.84-5.34), I2 82%; crude counts with nothing adjusted (Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). Recomputed: all 38 crude category ORs in Table 1 reproduce from their counts within 0.006; exp(1.36) = 3.90, exp(0.5 x 1.36) = 1.97 and exp(0.9 x 1.36) = 3.40 as printed. A DerSimonian-Laird pooling of the ten per-study estimates read from Figure 3 gives 3.90 (2.84-5.35), I2 81.7%, reproducing the printed result, as do the subgroup totals. 'Category-level odds that did not rise steadily in several studies' is right: by Table 1, 6 of 10 studies have at least one exposed category below a lower one or below 1 (Tien 0.84 at moderate use; Swedish conscripts 0.56 and 0.98 at 1 and 2-4 occasions; Henquet 4.89 then 3.96; Miettunen 3.32 then 3.00; ALSPAC 3.11 then 1.42; GAP 0.70, 0.40, 0.65 before 1.24 and 3.51). The fitted curves of Figure 2, on which the authors base 'a consistent increase ... in all the included studies', are rising by construction (one log-linear slope per study). The exposure scales differ between studies: lifetime frequency, past-year frequency, duration of use, dependence, and in Dunedin age at first use (use by 15 ranked above use by 18). The diagnosis subgroup (5.07, 3.62-7.09) contains two studies only (Swedish conscripts and GAP); Arseneault's schizophreniform disorder is pooled with the symptom studies in Figure 3B, although Table 1 and the Results list it as a diagnosis. One of the ten datasets (GAP) is the authors' own, replaced with new data they supplied (Figure 1; Results, 1st paragraph). The authors write that a causal link cannot be unequivocally established (Discussion, 8th paragraph), while the abstract says high levels of use increase the risk; the claim's association wording ('found the odds ... rising') matches the evidence. Overlap: five of the six cohorts pooled here were published by 2006 (Tien 1990, Arseneault 2002, Zammit 2002, Henquet 2005, Wiles 2006) and are probably also among Moore et al.'s seven cohorts, so the two reviews are not independent replications (to be checked against Moore's list).

anchors.extracted: 18 studies in the systematic review, 10 in the meta-analysis with 66,816 participants. Random-effects pooled slope b 1.36 (95% CI 1.04-1.68), i.e. OR 3.90 (2.84-5.34) for schizophrenia and other psychosis-related outcomes in the most severe users against people who did not use; I2 82%.

Crude ORs recomputed from case and control counts at each level because studies adjusted for different covariates; people who used were ranked on a 0-1 scale with bins sized by group, never users at 0; individual data simulated from the summary counts and a logistic model fitted per study, exp(b) being the OR between the heaviest-ranked person (x = 1) and no use; pooled assuming an equivalent distribution of use across studies, weighted by the SE of b, DerSimonian-Laird random effects because I2 exceeded 50%.

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Level of Exposure, Cases, Total and OR (Crude) columns)
anchors.extracted: Category-level crude ORs do not rise steadily in 6 of 10 studies: Tien 0.84 (moderate) then 2.17 (daily); Swedish conscripts 0.56, 0.98, 1.90, 3.24, 6.71; Henquet 0.99, 2.18, 2.14, 4.89, 3.96; Miettunen 2.62, 2.82, 3.32, 3.00; ALSPAC 2.07, 3.11, 1.42, 5.69; GAP 0.70, 0.40, 0.65, 1.24, 3.51. Reference rows include 'No cannabis within last year' (Wiles) and 'No use at age 18' (Arseneault).

OR at other points of the ranking: median person who used at all 1.97 (1.68-2.31); median of the top 20% 3.40 (2.55-4.54). The authors state the 3.90 is the risk of the most severe user, not the average user in the top category, and that applying Moore et al.'s average 45% attenuation for full adjustment to the top-20% figure would give results comparable with Moore's 2.1 for heavy use.

Limitations stated: inclusive outcomes (psychotic experiences to admission with a psychotic disorder); no data on the interval between regular use and onset; mixed designs; no potency or period-of-use data; exposure measures of different kinds (frequency, duration, clinical diagnosis of use, abuse or dependence) pooled; estimates from raw (unadjusted) data, so confounding by ethnicity or socioeconomic status may explain part of the effect.

Subgroups: cohort 3.83 (2.34-6.29), six studies; cross-sectional 3.99 (2.50-6.37), four including the GAP case-control data; psychotic symptoms 3.59 (2.42-5.32), eight including Arseneault; diagnosis of psychosis 5.07 (3.62-7.09), two (Swedish conscripts, GAP). Per-study estimates from 1.85 (Tien) to 7.45 (Degenhardt). Meta-regression by year P = .53; Egger P = .79, Begg P = .86.

Recomputed: 1.97 (1.68-2.31) and 3.40 (2.55-4.54) follow from the slope and its interval.
All ten labels read the same on Figure 3A; Zammit 2011 shows 4.36 in panel A (the low-resolution panel B label is hard to read).

reporting_issues.note: From general knowledge, not from this paper: the German counts (2,437 participants) match the EDSP cohort reported by Henquet et al. in the BMJ in 2005, which is not in the reference list.
Confirmed by recomputation: the 5.07 (3.62-7.09) reproduces only from the two studies, and the 3.59 only with Arseneault among the symptom studies.
The 3.99 (2.50-6.37) reproduces only with GAP in the cross-sectional group.
Nuance: for the GAP case-control data the order rests on retrospective recall rather than being unknown; for the three surveys it is not established.
The y-axis of Figure 2 reads OR; the legend says estimated risk ratio.
References 4 (Lancet 2012;379:8) and 9 (Lancet 2009;374:8) carry the same kind of page field.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: protocol, excluded-study list, risk-of-bias assessment and its use in interpretation, and appropriate (adjusted) pooling are all missing; items 4 and 5 are close calls as the card says, and either reading leaves several critical flaws.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits; the quoted phrases (abstract; Discussion, 9th paragraph) and points (1) to (6) are accurate against the text and figures. One addition: the Methods state that never users were always the reference category, but Table 1 shows other reference groups in some studies (see missed).

missed: Reference groups: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph says never users were consistently the reference, but Table 1's reference rows are 'No cannabis within last year' (Wiles 2006), 'None' or 'No use' for frequency at baseline (Henquet 2005, Degenhardt 2001) and 'No cannabis use at age 18' (Arseneault 2002). The card's comparison field repeats the Methods statement; it should note the table, and claims should say 'against no use' rather than 'against never use'.

Crude absolute risks by level can be read from Table 1 for the six cohorts (editors' calculation; follow-up length not given in this paper): Swedish conscripts, admission for schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 (0.59%) with no use vs 28 of 731 (3.8%) with more than 50 occasions; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder by 26, 12 of 494 (2.4%) vs 3 of 29 (10.3%). The card's cannot_establish lists absolute risks, and the frequency claim says no source gives them; both should be qualified, with the caveat that these are crude.

In the Dunedin study the ordered levels are defined by age at first use (use by 18 vs use by 15, Table 1), so in one of the ten studies the 'level of use' is age of onset rather than amount; the exposure field's statement that age at first use was not considered needs that exception.

Overlap with Moore et al. (2007): five of the six pooled cohorts were published by 2006 (Tien 1990, Arseneault 2002, Zammit 2002, Henquet 2005, Wiles 2006), so Marconi and Moore probably share most of their cohort data (to be checked against sc_moore_2007). The two reviews should not count as independent replication in the frequency claim's status.
